panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Real transthoracic echocardiographic image demonstrating turbulent color flow in the aortic arch, a characteristic manifestation of aortic coarctation. B: Real echocardiographic suprasternal-window image directly shows focal narrowing of the aortic isthmus with a measured isthmus-to-proximal-arch ratio of 0.4. C: Real continuous-wave Doppler echocardiogram demonstrates high-velocity systolic flow across the coarctation site with a significant pressure gradient. D: Real echocardiographic image shows the caption-specified indirect finding of left ventricular hypertrophic remodeling associated with aortic coarctation; this specific finding is not in the controlled vocabulary and is recorded as a proposed finding.
panels.attribution_text: La Mura et al. Multimodality Imaging Approach in Diagnosis and Follow-Up of Aortic Coarctation in Adulthood.. Journal of clinical medicine 2026. doi:10.3390/jcm15030949. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Assessment of aortic coarctation by TTE. (A) Aortic arch colour imaging with turbulent flow in suprasternal window. (B) Narrowing of isthmus diameter (with arrow) compared to proximal aortic arch (ratio 0.4) in suprasternal window for anatomical assessment. (C) Continuous doppler showing peak systolic velocity (>2 m/s) and peak pressure gradient (>20 mmHg) across narrowing site for functional assessment of significant CoA gradient. (D) Indirect CoA finding of LV hypertrophic remodelling.
in_text_mentions: A suprasternal view allows for functional evaluation with continuous-wave doppler (CW) to assess peak systolic velocity (>2 m/s) and peak pressure gradient (>20 mmHg) across the CoA site and pulsed-wave doppler, demonstrating prolonged diastolic flow (diastolic tail) with high velocity (>1 m/s) due to downstream obstruction [25]. A subcostal view shows delayed (>50 ms from ECG R wave) and reduced (<55 cm/s) systolic upstroke velocity and the persistence of anterograde diastolic flow in the distal thoracic and upper abdominal aorta [26] (Figure 1).

plate_findings.evidence: Caption identifies significant coarctation of the thoracic aorta distal to the left subclavian artery; marked narrowing is visible at the indicated region.
Caption explicitly states poststenotic dilatation adjacent to the coarctation.
The panel is labeled "Coarctation" and shows collateral vessels along the thoracic aorta; the article text notes that very few collateral vessels were present.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Three-dimensional patient CT angiography directly demonstrates focal narrowing of the thoracic aorta distal to the left subclavian artery with poststenotic dilatation, characteristic of postductal coarctation. [raw subtype: postductal] B: This three-dimensional CT panel shows the focal aortic narrowing and collateral anatomy. The caption-supported hypoplastic abdominal aorta is not represented by a dedicated vocabulary term and is therefore listed as a proposed finding. [raw subtype: postductal] C: Coronal patient CT angiography visibly demonstrates severe postductal thoracic aortic narrowing, collateral vessels, and downstream aortic dilatation. The hypoplastic abdominal aorta is also captioned but lacks a vocabulary key. [raw subtype: postductal]
panels.attribution_text: Jurcut et al. Coarctation of the aorta in adults: what is the best treatment? Case report and literature review.. Journal of medicine and life 2011. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: CT 3D images showing significant coarctation of the thoracic aorta beyond the origin of the left subclavian artery (arrow) with poststenotic dilatation and hypoplastic abdominal aorta
in_text_mentions: For clearly defining the location and anatomy of the coarctation, the patient underwent CT angiography examination that confirmed the presence of the coarctation just distal to the left subclavian artery, with poststenotic dilatation of the descending aorta, with very few collateral vessels (Figure 4) and a hipoplastic abdominal aorta.
